t: Managing the Behavior of Public Frontline Employees through Change-Oriented Training: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment
abs: Most public frontline employees work out of sight of management. Direct management through authority and incentives is therefore often challenging. We argue that managers can rely on change-oriented training as an effective management tool that can affect employee behavior and work as an alternative or supplement to commands and incentives. First, we outline the concept of change-oriented training and explain how it can direct the behavior of public employees towards organizational goals and political priorities. Second, we test the effect of change-oriented training on employee behavior in a large-scale field experiment of teachers in Danish public schools. We show that training has a substantial effect on teachers’ behavior in the classroom and infer from this that training should be seen as a valuable management tool with the ability to influence the behavior of frontline employees.

t: Do Performance Metrics and Targets Boost Trust in Government?
abs: This book is a valuable contribution to the literature on performance measurement and targets, especially about how they relate to broader political systems. It advances an argument about the role of targets for political trust. In so doing, it synthesizes a broad range of theoretical perspectives. Performance targets are argued to have been adopted to address a crisis of trust in politics, through creating more robust mechanisms of accountability and monitoring. The targets help boost trust as the reduction of uncertainty and associated beliefs about politicians’ actions and motivations. This is especially important at a time when other more traditional sources of trust are no longer so prevalent. Boswell argues that targets about the outcomes of public policy are particularly effective in this regard because they relate directly to the concerns of citizens. However, her argument maintains, the use of targets is not straightforward. There are many well understood problems with their use. In this light, the main focus of the argument is about how, despite these problems, performance measurement remains embedded as a technique of public management. In this way, the systems are normalized as a way of framing policy problems and responses. They appear likely to endure both as techniques and influences on political communication and governance. They also seem likely to persist despite other challenges, such as a resurgence of populist politics and contemporary skepticism with some forms of expert judgment. The argument is interesting and more complex than the simple summary given above; the space available in this review cannot afford a full exposition of all the nuances. However, the early Chapters (especially Chapters 1 and 2) draw particularly on the sociology of science, reflecting the author’s considerable expertise in this area. These sections build on insights from the work of authors including Wendy Espeland (Espeland and Sauder 2007), Niklas Luhmann (Luhmann 1979), and Anthony Giddens (Giddens 1990). A particularly interesting feature is how these theories are blended with scholarship from public administration, especially work on new public management and performance management, and research from accounting on the growth in use of audits. The increased use of targets is also part of the trend toward greater use of public authority to “regulate” organizations in the public sector, often at arms-length. This regulation has grown at the same time as allowing organizations greater variety in their use of management practices and permitting greater diversity of organizational forms (such as public/private hybrids and firms delivering services under contract). The central claim of the book is that performance measurement was an attempt by government in the United Kingdom to reground trust through establishing precise and authoritative modes of signaling and monitoring about government performance. In this sense, the term “manufacturing” in the title reflects both how management tools are intended to produce an increase in trust and politicians’ attempts to persuade citizens about the benefits that they confer. Rather than helping political control, such as in the more conventional principal-agent perspective, Boswell’s argument places more emphasis on their symbolic role. This aspect of the argument draws in part on Michael Power’s “audit society” research showing how audits offer “rituals of verification” (Power 1997). The book aims to understand and explain rather than to produce recommendations for reform. The empirical material consists of expertly constructed case studies. These case studies draw on a variety of evidence including a range of government, parliamentary and other reports and interviews with actors involved in the systems. These sources are in places supplemented by quantitative measures, especially about the media coverage of targets. The cases focus primarily on the policy areas of immigration, asylum, and defence procurement since 2000 in the United Kingdom. Chapters 3, 4, and 5 explore the role of targets for monitoring in UK public administration and the role of information produced in contributing to political trust. The chapters are thorough and set out the processes and outcomes of the use of targets. The research carefully shows how, rather than increasing public trust, the systems have at times contributed to increasing cynicism and even distrust in government. The many problems in the target systems receive considerable attention. These include the unintended damaging consequences for trust between politicians and civil servants. Particularly interesting are the sections on how civil servants and organizations made sense of the measures, whether the measures were “coupled” to the broader practices of the departments or whether they were bypassed, and why the targets persisted given their limitations. The story about targets is consistent with the bigger picture of major challenges facing departments in the period, with sections of the Home Office’s activities relating to justice being hived-off to another department. This contextual change shows that departmental reorganization are used as a signal of policy intent in a way not dissimilar to Boswell’s discussion of the setting of targets. The later empirical chapters look at the broader implications of targets. Chapter 6 extends the discussion to how targets spill over into political credit and blame as well as the extent to which they build trust. The evidence for this discussion especially draws on newspaper media coverage of the targets. In this regard, the targets were not straightforwardly received by the media. At many times, there was a skeptical reception in reporting by the media and in responses by citizens both about the role of targets and the outcomes they reported. Chapter 7 looks at the way targets were involved in defining issues as being important topics on the policy agenda. Inevitably, the position of measures and targets is complex, and even their definition entails trying to separate them from broader statements of priorities that similarly might command public attention. For example, targets are themselves of different kinds (strategic level, operational, cascaded to lower level units within organizations) and can be difficult to match up with policy objectives as stated in policy documents, departmental business plans, ministerial speeches, and party manifesto commitments. Manifestos are potentially worthy of further investigation given their role as commitments to objectives to inform voters and provide benchmarks to hold politicians to account once they are in power. The book skilfully combines thought provoking discussion of theory with the evidence. Inevitably there are questions about generalisability of the argument given the aspects of the evidence that are specific to the United Kingdom and the particular policy sectors in the period chosen. Much of the United Kingdom is under strong centralized control by the political executive in Westminster and Whitehall. In this constitutional context, the link between targets and politics especially reflects the power of the Prime Minister and senior ministers and their occasional, often media focused, hyperactivity in policy making. The relationship between politics and targets differs in federal or separation of powers systems or at local level. As Boswell notes, immigration and asylum were highly politicized policy domains. However, that is a good justification for focusing attention on them, and there is broad relevance in the evidence put forward. It would be of further interest to synthesize the qualitative evidence with research that has shown the effects of performance information on citizens at the individual level. Research published in JPART in recent years, including in the 2016 Virtual Issue on Citizen-State Interactions in Public Administration Research (Jakobsen et al. 2016), has shown that citizens and other users’ reception of information about performance is not as straightforward as most public organizations producing the information tend to assume. The political context can set off motivated reasoning about information, especially that arising from recipients’ partisan affiliations (James and Van Ryzin 2016). Relatedly, a range of cognitive biases in how performance measures are interpreted have been identified (Andersen and Hjortskov 2016; Olsen 2017). This strand of work, influenced by political and cognitive psychology, questions whether numbers are always more convincing than more anecdotal reports about performance. More generally, it shows that assessments of the effects of performance reporting need to take into account individual biases, motivations, and the broader political context in which information is communicated. The role of the more symbolic aspects of politics as an explanation of the persistence of targets and measures may not fully satisfy readers who place more emphasis on the, arguably more concrete, outcomes of the distribution of benefits and costs of the systems. Boswell notes that there has been a de-emphasizing of targets since 2010 by UK Government across many areas. Given the fiscal constraints that have since adversely affected public services, an elected government would clearly expect performance against targets to be more challenging such that they would be more cautious in using them. The alternative of lowering targets is similarly likely to be unappealing to politicians. The brutal axing of the Audit Commission and some of the associated systems of performance assessment for local government in the United Kingdom is an example of a substantial rolling back of such systems. However, it is difficult to advance general arguments. In other areas, targets are alive and well. For example, even within the UK central government, there are systems of targets for all executive agencies that require annual reporting and are subject to external audit. The book acknowledges complexities of these kinds, which present a more general challenge for research on this topic. The last chapter in the book examines the role of targets in the context of rising populism and skepticism about the role of experts. As Boswell notes, writing the book in 2016 following the election of Donald Trump in the US and the UK’s referendum vote to leave the European Union, the future is difficult to predict. This is still the case, but the book’s overall conclusion that, despite the problems of performance measures, the systems are likely to remain an important part of the link between political claims and outcomes appears to be very reasonable. More generally, the book is highly commendable for showing how what might otherwise risk being dismissed as a narrow technical issue is in fact embedded in, and of importance to, broader political systems. Making these arguments is at the core of showing why public administration is such an important area for research. Relating public administration literature to sociological and similar perspectives, which is relatively unusual, further cements the likely enduring value of the book’s contribution.

t: The Public Administration Manifesto II: Matching Methods to Theory and Substance
abs: This essay introduces the articles in the public administration methods symposium that will appear in this and the next two issues of the Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory. Overall the articles present the need for a rigorous methodological pluralism in public administration where the methods used need to match the substantive questions asked. The symposium hopes to provide a spring board for a discussion of future methodological issues in public administration.

t: Researching Multilevel Governance: A Local Government Perspective
abs: Conceptual disputes on the definition of multilevel governance (MLG) seem never-ending. Most scholars, starting with Gary Marks (1992, 1993) in his early writings, link MLG to the emergence of the EU supranational polity (see also Piattoni 2010). Others, though, use the concept to capture more general processes of redefining the role of the state beyond the European context (for a recent review, see Tortola 2017). The risk, as stated by critics, is that “While multi-level governance has the virtue of being capable of being invoked in almost any situation, that is also its great problem. Any complex and multi-faceted political process can be referred to as multi-level governance” (Peters and Pierre 2004, 88). In this ongoing debate, Robert Agranoff, in Local Governments in Multilevel Governance, proposes an original and much needed local government perspective. In this work, MLG is conceptualized from the bottom up, that is, from the vantage point of local public authorities, and anchored to their concrete operational practices and everyday organizational challenges. More specifically, Agranoff conceives of MLG in relation to the changing role of local and regional governments vis-à-vis their national principals. At the turn of the twenty-first century, neoliberal reforms in policy and administration like New Public Management, privatization, and externalization of services led to an increasing decentralization of governmental functions and responsibilities, since relations with NGOs, private companies, stakeholder organizations, and the like could only be managed at the local level. These concomitant changes brought about a new MLG system scenario characterized by the intersection of increasingly complex vertical intergovernmental relations (IGRs) and horizontal networks between public institutions and private organizations. The core purpose of the book is in revealing and discussing the intergovernmental management challenges underlying this new scenario and the emerging local governments’ (LGs) new leadership therein. The underlying assumption is that, despite radical changes occurring in the shift from top-down government to horizontal governance networks, government functions and bureaucratic organizations are not going to be hollowed-out. Rather, an ongoing process of adaptation is taking place with LGs at the forefront; this is the locus where “networking power” (p. 143) crystallizes, that is, where the capacity to coordinate complex systems of relations with other governments and multiple nongovernmental actors takes shape. Seven challenges are singled out by Agranoff as part of a “public managerial agenda for LG within MLG” (p. 231). The first is inter-program system development, or the capacity of LGs to make joint decisions that address local governance problems with other levels of government and/or NGOs and other relevant actors. The second challenge is political power, an issue often overlooked by managerial literature that could nevertheless seriously jeopardize MLG relations. Politics, according to Agranoff, is continuously embedded in the strategies and actions of the actors engaged in MLG relations, from key agencies and interest groups (big P politics) to NGOs, community-level service agencies, professionals, and applied scientists (small p politics) who may enjoy non-negligible influence in the community. Third, knowledge management is considered in the sense of building appropriate knowledge platforms that involve MLG’s multiple entities. The fourth challenge is that of networking, that is, the necessity for LGs to make some form of purposive collaborative linkage or other relationship which can eventually evolve into a kind of network organization. The fifth is interoperability, that is, reciprocal communication and accommodation to achieve interactive working policies and operations. The sixth concerns the changing modes of working in administrative organizations which, because of the continuing connective impact of MLG, need to be more outward-oriented and less hierarchical. Last but not least, the challenges of globalization and global influences on LGs are explored as exemplified by the emergence of transnational governance networks that connect LGs in order to promote learning and cooperation, often on specific policy issues such as climate change mitigation or new technologies. Overall these seven challenges outline a developmental theory of governmental functions, bureaucratic organizations, and, more specifically, LGs in MLG systems. Interinstitutional networking and boundary-spanning are identified as the key mechanisms of change driving—successful—organizational adaptation to the new context. For these mechanisms to take place, Agranoff posits the necessity of the emergence of a new figure, the network manager. New Public Management theory had already advocated for a shift from Weberian rule-oriented and hierarchically constrained bureaucrats to business-like professional managers. The—partly—new model emerging in the MLG era is that of conductive or collaborative management in which public managers’ skills are primarily in boundary-spanning, that is, building effective personal relationships with a wide range of actors, managing programs in nonhierarchical decision environments through negotiation and bartering, and performing the role of policy/program entrepreneur to mobilize resources to solve problems. Based on Agranoff’s extensive empirical research on collaborative governance in the United States as well as on cross-national studies and existing literature on other countries, the analysis proposed in Local Governments in Multilevel Governance is of extreme interest to the multiple variants of policy scholars, from public administration specialists to those broadly interested in governance. It shows how the MLG concept can be fruitfully applied to make sense of processes of redefinition of the functions of governmental and bureaucratic institutions, and more specifically of LGs in different institutional settings beyond the EU. Complexity is not just vaguely evoked but analytically spelled out in terms of the MLG challenges that emerge from simultaneous processes of diminishing hierarchical IGRs on the vertical dimension and blurring of state–society boundaries on the horizontal dimension. Practitioners will find valuable insights when reflecting on their own MLG experiences and probably a source of inspiration for experimenting with new relational tools and practices. But the main merit of the book from my point of view is that of laying the foundations for a research agenda on the still under-explored link between MLG and LG. Agranoff conceptualizes this link essentially in terms of public management theory, yet a more political—and maybe critical—reading revolving around categories of legitimacy, participation, and accountability would also be in order. In this perspective, the challenges of MLG test the very essence of democratic political systems: How can LGs effectively fill perceived gaps in the legitimacy of policy-making processes in complex MLG systems? How do we establish effective participative venues for stakeholders and common citizens? And how do we not only manage services and benefits more efficiently but also make them more concretely accessible to different categories of users? More specifically, four themes emerge: electoral multilevel politics, transnational networking, the place of agency in changing administrative structures, and access to rights in complex MLG systems. Regarding politics, the book explicitly acknowledges the necessity of staying attuned to how power and interests can permeate MLG cooperative arrangements beyond electoral politics. Yet, electoral politics should also be factored in. MLG has been regarded as an opportunity for democracy, opening up new participative venues especially from below (e.g., Piattoni 2010); this tremendously enhances the importance of LGs which assume a key role in linking citizens to political institutions. However, “being within” the local community does not mean automatically “being connected to” the local community. Controversies about wicked policy issues such as refugee reception or the location of polluting facilities like incinerators often bring to light how the interests of stakeholders (NGOs and migrant advocacy groups in the first case, private companies and experts in the second) do not necessarily reflect concerns and negative attitudes among resident citizens. Political parties are key players in these local struggles around values and preferences, and they can impede or block the process of adaptation of local administrative structures to any MLG environment. As acknowledged in the book, “Whereas the opportunity to build local systems by networking and playing the interactive game exists for LGs in most of the world’s democratic systems, not all undertake such actions” (p. 70). Why some LGs embrace the challenges of MLG and react to them—although often in different and distinctive manners—while others stay put is an open question which cannot be answered from a public management theory but requires a more careful consideration of the divisions within local communities and the role of political parties in dealing with them. Linked to this point is that of the global mobilization of LGs. Going transnational is conceived by Agranoff as a sort of “MLG-induced” practice that LGs fulfill in order to efficiently address the local consequence of global challenges such as climate change. However, as suggested by empirical research on this topic, not all cities are engaged in transnational networking, even though this should in principle be beneficial to them. An alternative approach is that of looking at city networks as a political card that some cities decide to play in their struggles with national level authorities or in their attempts to build local coalitions with specific economic actors (e.g., renewable energy companies, banking foundations, etc.). We still lack an in-depth understanding of the conditions that concretely favor such participation and of the dynamics of cities’ engagement and disengagement in transnational networks. The third theme underlying the book is that of agency within changing institutional structures and MLG adaptive processes. As mentioned above, the emergence of a “connective” paradigm of public administrations is linked to the presence of network managers specializing in boundary-spanning and relational work. This opens intriguing and still-to-be-answered research questions: where do network managers come from? Which conditions make an administrative structure more open and receptive to these kinds of administrative professionals? How does networking power relate to other types of more conventional power, like administrative and political power? Again, we can imagine that all LGs would beneficiate from incorporating such professional skills, yet this is not always the case. Why some institutional structures are more open to these figures while others are not is a question that cannot be answered in a purely managerial perspective. The fourth and final theme that can be derived from a political reading of Agranoff’s MLG challenges is that of access to rights. The issue is partly touched upon in the book in terms of “network performance” (e.g., p. 251–2). In MLG systems, LGs establish links with multiple agencies and organizations in order to more efficiently serve clients’ needs. This pluralization of actors “places added local pressure to identify and organise services around the client and/or problem” (p. 13). Yet, if for any—maybe political—reason LGs fail to deal with such pressure, navigating multiple public and private programs is likely to become a burden for citizens, with the risk of hampering access to rights for those least endowed with economic and cognitive resources. Unmanaged complexity and its consequences represent the other side of the coin of emerging MLG systems, a less positive facet that current research does not seem to have systematically addressed. Hence, if the anchoring of MLG to LGs’ structures and administrative practices is indeed a breakthrough which overturns the top-down bias underlying much of EU-focused research on MLG, the profound political implications of MLG challenges still remain to be explored. To this end, a greater dialogue between managerial and political science perspectives would indeed be helpful; it would allow a better understanding of how MLG affects the functioning of democratic political systems, including their modes of legitimacy and channels of political participation, therefore going beyond the limited focus on governments’ administrative capacity.

t: Does Collaboration Improve Organizational Efficiency? A Stochastic Frontier Approach Examining Cities’ Use of EECBG Funds
abs: Despite an abundance of research on collaboration, relatively little attention has been paid to the impact of collaboration on organizational outputs. This study helps fill this gap by unveiling the efficiency implications of collaborative arrangements. Using stochastic frontier (SF) analysis, we evaluate the efficiency of U.S. cities’ use of Energy Efficiency Conservation Block Grant (EECBG) funds in implementing sustainability programs and the extent to which collaboration influences resulting efficiency levels. The findings indicate the presence of considerable inefficiency in cities’ use of EECBG dollars. However, cities’ collaboration with a greater variety of governmental and community organizations is found to reduce this inefficiency, supporting the positive effects of collaborative partnerships in public policy implementation and management. Collaboration’s efficiency-improving effects are, however, not linear; its marginal effects diminish as cities approach the highest levels of collaboration. This implies that while collaboration brings a positive impact on achieving cost-efficient organizational outcomes, there is an optimal level of collaboration for cities to engage in.

t: When Your Group Fails: The Effect of Race-Based Performance Signals on Citizen Voice and Exit
abs: In recent years, performance-based accountability reforms have become widespread—particularly in the public education system—as a means of enhancing service delivery and citizens’ knowledge of and engagement with government. While an ever-growing literature has considered the overall effects of these administrative systems, few have fully considered the effect these have on underlying subgroups of relevance and inequalities in responses across these groups. In this article, we examine how citizens of various racial subgroups respond when governments send negative race-based signals about the performance of in- and out-racial groups. Specifically, we explore whether No Child Left Behind’s (NCLB) race-based failure signals affect racial groups’ use of voice in school board elections and their use of exit from local public schools. To do so, we combine school and voter administrative records in North Carolina with a regression discontinuity design that leverages exogenous variation around NCLB’s race-based school failure cutoffs. Consistent with our theoretical framework, we find that white and black citizens respond differently to race-based failure signals. We find the whites are more responsive overall: responding to failure signals of various types both by voting in local school board elections and exiting local failing schools. African Americans, however, seem much more sensitive to racialized cues—responding at the ballot box but not by exiting when their group fails. These results show that while performance accountability systems have broader effects than previously realized: shifting the composition of local elections and distorting the racial makeup of schools.
