t: Are Public Sector Managers a “Bureaucratic Burden”? The Case of English Public Hospitals
abs: Although managers are, globally, a central part of the new public management reform agenda, in recent years, policy makers and the media have raised concerns about their effectiveness and contribution. In some countries, notably the United Kingdom and the United States, this debate has been heavily influenced by Public Choice Theory (PCT), which depicts “bureaucrats” as rent seeking, self-serving individuals. In this study, focusing on the case of acute care hospital trusts in the English National Health Service, we formally test whether public sector managers represent a “bureaucratic burden.” Using a longitudinal database spanning six years (2007–2012) and employing a dynamic panel data model, the findings reveal that, contrary to PCT assumptions, managers do not engage, in the main, in rent seeking behavior and, crucially, appear to have a positive impact on organizational performance. Implications for theory, policy, and practice are discussed.

t: Keeping Your Enemies Close: The Role of Distrust in Structuring a Local Hydraulic Fracturing Policy Network in New York
abs: Explaining the mechanisms that structure policy networks is an important subject of public management research as networks are key mechanisms of convening actors across public, private, and nonprofit sectors to design and implement public policies. Previous research focuses on the positive role of trust in building network structures in the context of social service delivery. But many policy networks can be adversarial, particularly those that operate in a regulatory context. We know little about the role of distrust in building network structures in this context. This study conceptualizes distrust as a distinct concept from the absence of trust, and examines why stakeholders stay connected with distrusted stakeholders in a regulatory policy network. Using a mixed-method analysis of a local hydraulic fracturing policy network in New York, we found that actors stay connected with stakeholders they distrust to perform information processing, bridging, and demarcating operations, which in turn create reciprocating, bridging and/or bonding structures. Our findings suggest three implications for public management research relevant to both regulatory and service networks: distrust can create network connectivity, connectivity can structure networks in particular ways, and brokers do not reduce transaction costs if they lack skills in principled engagement.

t: A Timely Addition in the Study of Narrative
abs: Sandford Borins and Beth Herst’s new book, Negotiating Business Narratives: Fables of Information Technology, Automobile Manufacturing and Financial Trading Industries, systematically distills the contemporary narratives associated with the three business sectors identified in the title of the book. In contrast to the historically dominant interpretive narrative approaches to public administration and policy (e.g., Dodge, Ospina, and Foldy 2005), the approach in this research is rooted in classical structural narratology. Such an approach situates this text very much within recent trends in the study of narrative in public policy (e.g., Jones 2018). Structural approaches to narrative are explicitly deductive and theory driven and thus seek to identify narrative within different social, political, and institutional contexts toward the end of generalizable theory. As such, this research is focused narrowly on business industries, but the broader aim of the authors is to develop generalizable conceptions of narrative that are portable to different contexts. My read of this short text (78 pages) is that the authors have most certainly been successful on the first front and have taken the field another valuable step toward the second. Working from the structural premise of narratology, Borins and Herst efficiently detail their definition of private sector narratives in their opening chapter. Tapping much of the literature you would expect to see in this type of discussion (e.g., Bruner 1990; Propp 1968) the authors leverage and slightly modify Borins’ previous work (Borins 2011), which focused on public-sector narratives. The business industry operationalization of Borins’ previous work identifies three salient aspects of narrative: the protagonist of the narrative, society, and the corporate entity, where each is understood as either winning or losing. The winning and losing binary allows for each aspect to be understood as an independent narrative dimension. Intersecting the three dimensions produces an eight-cell analytic matrix—or what might just as easily be understood as eight archetypal business industry narratives ranging from corporate nirvana where all three aspects are winners to corporate nightmare where everyone losses. Using this deductive three-dimensional coding scheme, the authors then proceed to describe their data. In terms of which narrative patterns the authors are interested in, they focus on three business industries: information technologies, automobile manufacturing, and the financial trade industry. Across those three industries, they examine 35 years of US films, TV series, books, and similar narrative texts. To be selected for inclusion a text must have clearly identified a protagonist, focused on the protagonist’s experience with an organization or industry, and needed to have a “significant cultural profile” (p. 10). This sifting process produced a total of 63 texts across the three business industries (a full list, by industry, is provided in an appendix). The next three chapters of the book focus on the dominant narrative patterns identified for each of the three industries. Chapter 2 details the authors’ findings related to the information technology (IT) business industry. Most readers should be at least vaguely familiar with some of the narratives captured in the individual films, books, and the like that were coded for this chapter of the book. These stories include the rise of Apple and Microsoft, with the central roles of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs, as well as their relationship to one another. The chapter also captures the rise of more recent tech companies including Amazon, Google, Facebook, Twitter, and Uber. Borins and Herst find that the nirvana fable is the dominant narrative in the IT industry. The generic arc of this story is that there is an incredible idea proffered by a protagonist who flaunts normal business conventions, the idea gets noticed and garners support from investors, and consumers benefit from having access to the idea. In this story everyone wins. This chapter also identifies two recessive narratives including the thrown-over partner and the nightmare of the failed IT startup. Chapter 3 focuses on narrative findings related to the auto industry. Their findings here show that the narratives about the auto industry do not neatly cluster predominantly in one of the eight cells. Despite the lack of a dominant narrative, Borins and Herst identify a common thread throughout the coded narratives. They observe that regardless of which cell a narrative was coded into there is a common thread among most that made the CEO of the auto company a focal point of the narrative. While there are several references to the importance of auto industry CEOs within the chapter, several characters receive more attention than others, including Lee Iaocca’s turnaround at Chrysler, Alan Mulally’s success at Ford, GM Roger Smith’s dubious depiction by Michael Moore in Roger and Me, and Elon Musk’s characteristically positive depiction with Tesla. Chapter 4 details the narrative findings of the finance industry. For this collection of narrative data, the dominant narratives are overwhelmingly about “corporate wrong doing” (p. 38). Much of the data for this industry were familiar to me as I suspect they will be for many who read this book—including high profile documentaries such as Inside Job and films such as The Big Short, Margin Call, and the Wolf of Wall Street. Categorizing these stories into the eight cells, Borins and Herst observe tales of corporate rip-offs, inside jobs, and, most frequently, the corporate nightmare. The authors identify only two finance industry narratives that show favorably. The authors generalize about their findings observing that “…in their own way each of these narratives manifests tensions between individual agency, systemic failure (corruption and dysfunction), and complexity” (p.44). The concluding chapter of the book, Chapter 5, is a brief summary of the chapters that also preemptively speaks to potential criticisms such as noting that their study does not seek to “prove the social impact of the narratives it analyzes” (p.59). The authors conclude by arguing that their approach is broadly applicable, beyond that of the three business industries examined here. The research presented by Borins and Herst is conveyed in a well-written fashion and notable in its brevity. Indeed, the individual chapters are presented in an engaging style of prose that help their research findings glow with a slight aura of entertainment, which no doubt is assisted by the popularity of their subject matter. The brevity is also a strength, as it is uncharacteristic of narrative research more generally to tell short stories about stories. There is, however, one issue to which I would like to draw the reader’s attention. By the time I finished reading the book, I found myself wanting more information about how the data were coded, as the lack of clarity can at times undercut the thrust of some of the findings. For example, in chapter 3 the authors draw a distinction between the CEO of the auto industry (e.g., Lee Iacocca) as the “center who changes everything” (p. 25) and the process-focused IT stories, where these industries are found to have less central CEO type characters, yet they too also seem to feature incredibly central personalities such as Bill Gates and Steve Jobs. This is a distinction used by the authors to characterize the main difference between the IT and auto industry’s meta-stories, but without clearly harkening back to the coding that brought the distinction about, the difference between the two is less compelling than it could have been. There are similar issues elsewhere; however, given the wide range of acceptable narrative coding techniques that exist, I could hardly label this a fatal flaw. I think of it more as a niggling hindrance that slightly enervates the overall potency of the findings. Despite the issue mentioned above, I think this book has much to recommend. Analyzing popular culture narratives, this research effectively describes the narratives of three business industries. It does this quite well. The research also aspires to being generalizable to other contexts. Borins’ earlier work (Borins 2011) certainly helps make the case for generalizability, yet there is probably not enough specifically within this work to indicate the approach is truly generalizable. Still, there is quite enough to entice a potential narrative researcher to give it a try. The theoretical approach is clear and would no doubt be easy enough to replicate. While it never aspires to answer questions addressing the actual influence of narratives, on whom, by whom, or how individuals might come to accept or reject those narratives, it does tantalizingly provoke such questions and at least intimates how one might go about trying to answer them. In this sense, this research should garner the most attention from public administration and policy scholars with general interest in the study of narrative and, more narrowly, by those interested in the narrative intersection of the public sector and business. The former makes it a keeper for my bookshelf. The latter likely only applies to a niche audience of JPART’s readership, but, given a national and global circumstance characterized by almost instant information flows and increasingly complex interactions between business and government, I suspect interest in the narrative intersection between business and the public sector will only increase.

t: The Causal Effect of Public Service Motivation on Ethical Behavior in the Public Sector: Evidence from a Large-Scale Survey Experiment
abs: Public service motivation (PSM) and ethical behavior are central concerns in public administration. Yet, experimental evidence on the causes of ethical behavior and the causal effects of PSM remains scarce, curtailing our understanding of both. This article draws on a novel survey experimental design to improve this understanding. The design is based on a simple insight: asking about PSM can render salient PSM-oriented identities of respondents. By randomizing the order of PSM and outcome questions, PSM may be exogenously activated among survey respondents, and the causal effects of this activation assessed. Drawing on this design and a sample of over 5,000 Chilean central government employees—the largest experimental PSM survey sample to date—we find that PSM activation enhances willingness to report ethical problems to management. This provides the first experimental evidence that PSM may promote ethical behavioral intent, and suggests that activating public employees’ PSM can benefit public sector ethics.

t: From Ideology to Evidence: Publicness, Organizational Functioning, and School Teaching Climates
abs: Over the last 25 years, the growth of charter schools has been matched by the controversy associated with them. Supporters argue that charters overcome the bureaucratic weaknesses inherent in traditional public schools to drive innovation, increase school accountability, and encourage teacher and principal leadership, resulting in improved school effectiveness and student learning. Critics argue that charter schools are characterized by insufficient regulation and a hyper-focus on standardized testing that reduces equity, while draining traditional public schools of already low levels of resources. The arguments are strong and forceful, with theory and research findings readily available to back up both sides. But overall, the findings are as mixed and controversial as the competing theories and perspectives behind them. Zachary W. Oberfield’s thoughtful analysis, Are Charters Different? Public Education, Teachers, and the Charter School Debate, serves as a welcome departure from more ideological and polarizing literature on charter schools with its balanced, evidence-based analysis of organizational issues in charter schools. Grounded in the notion of publicness, Oberfield acknowledges the foundation of the charter school movement as the belief that an organization’s publicness—in terms of control, funding, and ownership—has an influence on its operations and seeks to assess this in the context of teaching climates. In so doing, his scholarship contributes beyond the education literature and charter school debates to the broader public management literature. This book has many strengths, including its grounding in theory, national sample of respondents, longitudinal perspective, and efforts to identify key distinctions within the charter sector. Oberfield offers generalizability, depth, and attention to changes over time by analyzing survey data from multiple sources and, in some cases, multiple rounds of data collection: (1) four rounds of the Schools and Staffing Survey (SASS), intermittently conducted from 1999 to 2012 nation-wide by the National Center of Education Statistics; (2) two rounds of the Teaching, Empowerment, Leading, and Learning (TELL) survey conducted by the New Teacher Center (NTC) in six states from 2012–2014; and (3) the Delaware Teachers Survey (DTS) conducted by Oberfield during the 2014–2015 academic year. The focus on national, school-level survey data from the SASS dataset provides a representative sample, which is supplemented by the other datasets to fill in gaps and provide additional context. These datasets are not equally representative, however, so it is important for the reader to keep in mind which findings are supported by the national sample and which may be more limited geographically. In addition, these survey programs cover different time periods, ranging from 1999 to 2015, so variability among the three survey program findings could reflect changes over time that are not directly comparable. Interestingly, Oberfield outlines his potential biases in the preface, identifying himself as having a long family history in support of public education, including teacher unions, but also a long-standing recognition of the challenges and lack of alternatives for high minority, urban schools. As the book unfolds, the reader may wonder if Oberfield initially hoped his straightforward analysis would confirm the arguments of charter critics. Instead, he finds and reports that many of the most vocal fears surrounding charters are relatively unfounded, at least in the context of teaching climates. If the author was hoping otherwise, he seems to have successfully set aside those biases throughout most of the text. The concluding chapter may offer some exception, where he tempers the significance of his own work, questioning the systemic impact of charter schools and sustainability of current differences in charter teaching climates, and at one point posing a question based on the assumption that future research will side with charter critics—areas clearly beyond the scope of his analysis. Overall, however, his efforts to put potential biases aside and focus on the results of his analyses are commendable. As Jeffrey R. Henig praises in the book’s foreword, “Zach Oberfield is thoughtful and deliberate, a modest scholar himself who wrestles with the evidence and presents it to readers fairly and clearly, despite the winds of political controversy that still rage around the charter school issue” (p. xiii). Charter schools, in theory, enjoy increased autonomy in exchange for increased accountability. The first two chapters set the stage, providing a brief overview of charter schools and the debates surrounding them, describing the study’s research methods, and identifying the theoretical underpinnings of the charter experiment, which include discussions of publicness (Bozeman 2004) and the application of public choice theory (Chubb and Moe 1990). Oberfield is careful to balance out theoretical expectations with a healthy skepticism, including discussions of professionalism and agency theory to support arguments that charters may not fulfill the expectations held for them. Chapter three describes characteristics of schools, students, and teachers in both charter and traditional public (subsequently “public”) schools across the period of study. Chapters four through eight present the heart of the findings on the autonomy-accountability trade-off (chapter four), teacher leadership and collaboration (chapter five), working conditions and turnover (chapter six), parent and community engagement (chapter seven), and teacher–administrator relationships (chapter eight). Oberfield concludes with a summary of major findings, implications for theory, and recommendations for school leaders, policymakers, and advocates (chapter nine). Within these chapters, he explores differences and similarities between public and charter schools, as well as distinctions within the charter school sector, specifically in relation to franchising, tax status, and strength of state charter laws. Beginning with an analysis of demographic characteristics, Oberfield paints a more moderate picture than what we typically see in the literature. One of the key arguments against charter schools is that they take the best students from traditional public schools and avoid educating those most in need. While demographic characteristics are an imperfect proxy for analyzing such claims, they are commonly used on both sides, and Oberfield’s measured assessment is informative. When controlling for other factors, he finds few statistical differences between charter and public schools in terms of race but some differences in terms of English language learners (ELL), students with limited English proficiency (LEP), and students with individual education plans (IEP). These differences were more moderate than many charter critics suggest, however, with later waves of the SASS survey suggesting a convergence in some areas over time. Moving beyond demographics, Oberfield explains the “bargain” at the heart of charter schools—more autonomy in exchange for greater accountability—and the hope of some supporters that this trade-off trickles down from the school level to the teacher level (p. 65). He ultimately finds mixed results, with charter teachers reporting greater autonomy in some areas, less red tape, and innovative school environments. Data also suggest higher levels of accountability for charter teachers in terms of high standards, objective assessment, and accountability to department chairs. Analyses fail to demonstrate, however, greater levels of accountability in terms of consequences or accountability to local school districts. As Oberfield points out, some of the variability in findings may be due to teacher perceptions. I would argue that findings may also reflect the complexity of the accountability construct more broadly. It is easy for citizens and policymakers to say they want to see schools more “accountable” for educating students, but the devil is in the details. Accountable to whom—parents, internal managers, the central office, policymakers, the state? At what level—school or teacher? And how measured—standardized test scores, graduation rates, student enrollment? While Oberfield makes a worthy effort to contribute to this debate with the available survey items, it is important to keep the complexity of the accountability construct in mind. Teacher leadership and collaboration are related rationales for charter schools. While in some ways counter-intuitive to the teacher autonomy argument, increased opportunities for teacher leadership and collaboration move authority from the district or school level to the teacher level. Oberfield’s analysis clearly supports the notion that charter teachers carry out more leadership in their schools than public teachers, but differences appear to be narrowing over time and findings with regard to collaboration with other teachers are mixed. Resource constraints are one of the key challenges for charter schools recognized by some supporters and critics alike. With charter school funding based on voluntarily enrolled student numbers, often at lower per pupil levels than nearby schools and in many cases lacking existing physical infrastructure, competing with public school salaries is thought to be an ongoing challenge and mitigating factor in the charter school experiment. Oberfield’s analysis provides data to this discussion, finding that yes, indeed, charter school teachers work more hours for less money, though this does not translate into less satisfaction, increased burnout, or greater turnover rates. As Oberfield suggests, it may be that charter teachers do not realize the pay gap or prioritize the increased autonomy and leadership opportunities to greater pay. Parent and community engagement are argued to play an important role in student success, and charter schools are known for leveraging and even requiring high levels of engagement and parent volunteering. The study’s findings support this reputation, suggesting that charter schools demonstrate more engagement with parents and communities than their public counterparts. This discussion is tempered, however, with Oberfield’s important recognition that self-selection and unobserved differences may play a critical role in this area—an argument frequently made by charter critics but beyond the scope of these data sets. The importance of leadership and the notion that management matters are two areas that have also played a prominent role in arguments for educational reform broadly over the years. Oberfield’s analysis considers this in the context of performance management, finding that publicness is conversely related to the formal evaluation of teachers, the use of student test scores in teacher evaluations, and timely availability of assessment information. While the use of teacher evaluations is considered a best practice across sectors, I would argue that the findings related to student assessments support arguments of both sides. Reform advocates often emphasize the importance of focusing on outcomes, including expectations for teachers to deliver high test scores (Hanushek 2011), whereas critics denounce the overemphasis on test scores as inappropriate measures for assessing teacher quality and for the displacement of other important goals (Ravitch 2013). The central finding of Oberfield’s analysis of public and charter schools does not provide the attention-grabbing headlines that either side of the argument would like, but it makes up for the lack of excitement by providing credible evidence to better inform the charter school debate: “[C]harter schools have made strides toward meeting the goals set by early advocates. But they haven’t completely fulfilled their promise” (p. 184). Are Charters Different? does not stop with these intersectoral comparisons; it also looks inside the charter sector to explore whether franchising, tax status, or the strength of state charter laws explain variability within the sector as part of each chapter. While there are few significant findings reported here, the lack of such findings and an unexpected finding have important implications for the charter debate. For example, in terms of the profit motive, the relationship between publicness and red tape was significant but counter-intuitive, as charter teachers in schools with for-profit educational management organizations perceive more red tape than teachers in nonprofit managed charters. In terms of legislation, state charter laws are thought to serve as important sources of support or barriers to charter autonomy, but Oberfield’s findings did not find significant differences in teaching climate based on the strength of state charter laws. This is an important finding for the charter debate, but one that requires more examination. While it is possible that legislation is not important to organizational climates, as Oberfield suggests as a possible explanation, it may also be possible that federal legislation, such as the No Child Left Behind legislation prominent during the survey distribution periods, mitigates the influence of state charter laws and levels the playing field to some extent across states. It may also be that overall rankings mask the most influential elements of state charter laws. With a discussion that emerges clearly from his preceding analyses, Oberfield recommends that public school leaders consider ways to reduce red tape for teachers, empower them with more autonomy and leadership, and foster deeper levels of parent and community engagement. While the findings generally support charter school claims, he cautions charters that some elements are lacking, including the promise of greater accountability and improvements in teacher collaboration. Circling back to some of his original, valid concerns that “experiments are driven more by a priori assumptions and ideology than by careful analysis and evaluation” (p. 197), he reminds us of the importance of understanding organizational forms and calls for more nationally representative research, additional questions on national education datasets, the use of more longitudinal data, and attention to scale. With significance beyond public education, Oberfield’s analysis contributes to the broader debate on public–private management, providing support for the argument that publicness can impact organizational functioning. Despite its value in this arena, I would argue that more grounding in the literature would have strengthened this text as an academic resource. The book cuts to the chase, outlining key findings for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers in an easy to understand format, but I found myself wanting more depth on the literature review and subsequent discussion of findings, both on charter schools and related public management theory. While the book clearly presents findings and brings in related theoretical frameworks, the data’s richness allows for a much deeper theoretical dive, with the potential to make even more significant contributions to public management theory. The findings do provide important lessons, however, and raise interesting questions for public managers and scholars beyond education. Building on Oberfield’s recommendations for charter school leaders and researchers, I would advocate for related recommendations for public management scholarship more broadly, including continued analysis of public management questions in the context of schools. Some of Oberfield’s findings support long-standing bodies of public management work, such as the desire to reduce unnecessary red tape and foster leadership capacity in public managers. Other findings provide insights for more contemporary scholarship or unexpected findings worth exploring. First, Oberfield’s findings around teacher pay and satisfaction are counter to what public service motivation theory would predict. What is motivating these charter school teachers, and what are the implications for motivation in public and nonprofit agencies more broadly? Second, what lessons can public administrators learn from the ability of charter schools to demonstrate greater levels of parent and citizen engagement? While some of this may be due to self-selection as critics warn, are there efforts or activities that public managers should adopt in toolkits for stakeholder and community engagement? Third, can educational research help us tease out the complexity of accountability in public organizations? What contributions can schools make to our understanding of the relationship between accountability mechanisms and publicness, management practices, and other factors? Finally, public management scholars should pay more attention to the impact of time and organizational age. Oberfield’s work identifies areas where public-charter differences appear to be converging. Are some of our long-standing beliefs about public–private differences influenced by organizational age to a greater extent than we have acknowledged? The strengths of Are Charters Different? clearly outweigh its weaknesses using national, longitudinal data with broad generalizability to provide a balanced and evidence-based assessment of public and charter schools in the context of teaching climates that is grounded in theory. The final product is an instructive analysis of charter school teaching climates that both supporters and critics should read to better inform the current prescriptive debates. From a public affairs focus, the work raises interesting questions and demonstrates the value of public–private management research in the context of schools, which offer a large sample of organizations with the same, or at least similar, fundamental purpose, but a variety of “publicness” variables, including ownership, control, and funding.

t: Executive Control and Turnover in the Senior Executive Service
abs: If presidents wish to see their policy priorities implemented, they need control over key decision-making positions often occupied by career executives. This article examines whether political conflict with a new administration drives career executives from their positions. This can happen because presidents target specific individuals or because career professionals anticipate conflict and strategically exit before a new president takes office. To assess this dynamic, we use novel data that combine individual survey responses with personnel records to analyze the probability that an agency executive departs her position from March 2015 to July 2017. Given our findings that turnover is driven by both presidential marginalization and strategic exit by bureaucrats, we conclude with implications for presidential efforts to control the bureaucracy.

t: Causal Inference Methods: Lessons from Applied Microeconomics
abs: This paper discusses causal inference techniques for social scientists through the lens of applied microeconomics. We frame causal inference using the standard of the ideal experiment, emphasizing problems of omitted variable bias and reverse causality. We explore how laboratory and field experiments can succeed and fail to meet this ideal in practice. We then outline how different methods and the statistical assumptions behind them can lead to causal inference in non-experimental contexts. We explain when problems with omitted variables bias can and cannot be addressed using observed controls. We consider tools for studying natural experiments, including difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity techniques. Finally, we discuss additional concerns that may arise such as weighting, clustering, multiple inference, and external validity. We include Stata code for implementing each of these methods as well as a series of checklists for researchers detailing important robustness and design checks. Throughout, we emphasize the importance of understanding the context of a study and implementing analyses in a way that acknowledges strengths and limitations.

t: Bolstering Democracy or Illustrating Performance? Contracting Out Public Participation
abs: Public administration scholars have long been interested in contracting out and the management of public sector contracts. Early empirical work focused on determining whether using contractors was more cost efficient than public provision (Savas 1977). In more recent years, scholars have investigated how transaction costs and principal-agent problems affect both the decision to contract out and the day-to-day management of contracts (Brown and Potoski 2003; Girth 2014). In other studies, authors have examined how the use of contracts has affected public sector equity goals (Fernandez, Malatesta, and Smith 2013). As a result, much of the existing empirical research on contracting out has been an effort to either (a) assess whether contracting out is efficient or (b) determine how to use contracts as policy implementation tools. In Citizen Participation in the Age of Contracting, Anna Amirkhanyan and Kristina Lambright contribute a new empirical perspective to the study of public sector contracting. Noting that one of the key roles of democratic public administration is to serve as a critical link between citizens and government, Amirkhanyan and Lambright assess how the presence of contractors affects citizen participation in public programs. Studying health and human services contracts, they investigate which forms of participation local governments employ, the degree to which participation and feedback affect public programs, the barriers that inhibit participation, and the motives that managers have for engaging with the public. Since many contractors, particularly those in health and human services, are responsible for delivering public services, it is important to understand how this added layer of “governance” has affected the public’s ability to participate in public programs and the implications for democratic government. Their research is timely, as nations around the world attempt to reconcile the accessibility of information with low trust in government, perceived performance shortcomings, and complex public problems. Scholars have long suggested that the use of contractors could theoretically pervert democratic administration, as private firms are not beholden to the people and public values in the same ways as public organizations (Moe 1987). Amirkhanyan and Lambright conducted nearly 100 interviews with public and private contract managers across six eastern US states to determine empirically how the use of contractors affects democratic participation in public programs. Using semi-structured conversations, they were able to probe deeply for details about participation mechanisms, building a robust dataset that provides strong supporting evidence for their findings. Asking both public managers and contractors for their perspectives on participation allows for direct comparison of sectoral priorities and approach. Along the way, Amirkhanyan and Lambright expertly link public administration scholarship on participation and contracting, generating interesting, solidly grounded findings that could serve as a critical starting point for following theoretical and empirical inquiry in these areas. They also raise important questions about the role of citizens in governance and the effectiveness of methods that governments are using to try to preserve the bottom-up elements of democracy. Despite longstanding rhetoric espousing the benefits of democracy, much of US political history has been an effort to determine who is qualified to participate and in what ways. With the rise of New Public Management and its associated efforts to mimic business processes and leverage market forces, citizens were re-cast as clients. As a result, the roles of both the government and citizens changed dramatically, shifting from street-level bureaucracy and direct democracy to indirect network management and sporadic information sharing. In Citizen Participation in the Age of Contracting, Amirkhanyan and Lambright argue that these changes may have important implications for how citizens are able to participate in and influence government, especially regarding accountability, transparency, power, and trust. They begin by investigating whether the use of contractors has changed the mechanisms that are used to engage citizens. They find widespread use of more traditional means of public engagement, including public meetings, advisory boards, and formal data collection mechanisms, such as client surveys, interviews, and site visits. There is little evidence of innovation or the use of high-intensity participation approaches. Instead, participation seems to be used in a one-time, one-way exchange designed to aid with operational problems such as identifying service quality tweaks and making changes in response to client preferences. Amirkhanyan and Lambright label this as “thinking inside the box,” holding that “counties and contractors seemed to be primarily interested in soliciting information about citizens’ experiences and views, rather than granting citizens greater control and decision-making power” (p. 73). Thinking inside the box might not be a problem if the feedback received through participation is used to generate meaningful changes to public programs. Taking this next logical step, Amirkhanyan and Lambright investigate the types and impact of citizen feedback. They find that positive feedback, general comments of appreciation, and relatively simple comments are more commonly generated than negative or more substantive input. This may indicate that feedback is being used to make minor changes to programs based on citizen needs. There are important sectoral differences, as contractors tend to focus on service delivery changes while governments use citizen feedback to inform their management of the contractor or to guide funding decisions. As a result, the authors note that when contractors lead participation initiatives “community members appear to have considerably less impact on program planning and design” (p. 92). Participation under contracting may be used to facilitate tinkering at programmatic margins rather than substantive democratic contributions. One possible explanation might be that democratic citizen participation is difficult in practice, especially when contractors have a short-term commitment from government. To this end, Amirkhanyan and Lambright investigate the challenges that contractors face when engaging citizens. They find that, though there are challenges to participation such as the cost and the utility of responses, they are not as intractable as previous studies might indicate. Contractors report problems with low response rates, client reluctance, and a lack of staff appreciation while government managers note that they had problems managing process conflicts, ensuring the representativeness of the input gathered, and dealing with mixed feedback. But, across all interviews, these problems were not frequently reported. As in other areas, contractors focus on more mechanistic service delivery problems while government remains concerned about more democratic elements of participation. Amirkhanyan and Lambright close their book with a discussion of the purpose of citizen engagement in governance. Participation efforts are designed to improve service quality, ensure responsiveness, and increase the understanding of client needs. However, public organizations are much more likely to report concerns about empowerment and program quality while contractors are more interested in responsiveness and meeting external requirements. Amirkhanyan and Lambright conclude that, under contracting, managerial motives tend to dominate the practical use of participation mechanisms. Though governments retain an interest in promoting democratic concerns, contractors have different objectives. Ultimately, the authors assert that efforts to engage citizens “fall far short of reaching the ideals of democracy and self-governance” (p. 142). Amirkhanyan and Lambright present a thorough and well-reasoned book that addresses many interesting questions about how citizens participate in the era of contracting. Their research is primarily descriptive, in keeping with research traditions in public management that emphasize exploring what is happening before addressing causation. However, because of this approach, the impetus is on subsequent scholarship to attempt to investigate the factors that influence and cause changes in participatory governance. Similarly, additional work is needed to expand the validity of the findings to different contexts, as their research is limited to a few cases in eastern US states. And though they present some recommendations on how to address participation problems, supporting evidence is incomplete as causal pathways are not explored. Finally, the book does not provide insight into how citizens experience differences when interacting with government and contractors. As a result, many noteworthy questions remain. This book should serve as a foundational text for scholars interested in explaining how contractors affect both the planning and implementation of 21st century public programs. The book’s findings are not particularly surprising given our understanding of the importance of client services in the for-profit and nonprofit sectors. Nonprofit organizations tend to prioritize their mission and the needs of the associated segments of the public (Gazley 2008; Malatesta and Smith 2014). For-profit firms have been shown to attend to the specific requirements of a contract, including the narrowly defined interests of those receiving services (Brown and Potoski 2003; Salamon 1993). Both types of organizations are likely to be primarily motivated by the desire to get the next contract. In such a context, it is not surprising that participation mechanisms are primarily concerned with characteristics of services delivery. The book leaves the reader with two primary questions. First, Amirkhanyan and Lambright adopt a decidedly bottom-up view of democracy. Is this the right interpretation of participation in the context of contracting? Taking this view, direct democratic participation should be a priority for administrators concerned with service quality and outcomes. However, the street-level bureaucrats, in this instance, are not government employees but contractors. Though there is a strong movement in the nonprofit literature to include nonprofits as street-level bureaucrats, questions remain over whether private organizations (for-profit or nonprofit) can be expected to set policy at the street-level (Brodkin 2012; Skelcher and Smith 2015). In particular, concerns remain over whether thinking of contractors as street-level government representatives subverts traditional democratic mechanisms and prioritizes profit or mission motivations. More scholarship is needed to determine how public objectives can be achieved when services are provided via contract. This begs the question of whether the presence of contractors matters in public service delivery. Despite evidence that contractors are not especially creative or concerned with democratic participation, Amirkhanyan and Lambright’s findings may indicate that contractors make little difference. Government managers, actively pursuing broader democratic objectives, report using participation to set strategy and steer service delivery. Contractors are focused on the quality of service delivery and customer needs. This breakdown of roles is what might be expected based on respective organizational priorities and areas of expertise. Many previous studies of public participation indicate that public administrators have long struggled to foster effective engagement. Given these enduring problems, the book’s findings might indicate that the inclusion of contractors is actually an improvement—even if it is at the margins. Though there is no evidence of groundbreaking democratic advances, service quality improvements may be important for increasing citizen satisfaction with government. However, it is also possible that the inclusion of contractors skews public participation in undesirable ways. If public organizations cede the responsibility for participation to contractors and allow private firms to determine the form and function of public input, the types of participation and the uses of the data gathered may change. Contractors, interested in demonstrating performance, might not pursue the same types of engagement as traditional public administrators. As a result, the intersection of democratic participation and contracted service delivery is a fertile area for future research. The book points the way toward three primary areas of additional scholarship. First, more research is needed to determine how public managers can influence participation under contracting. How can contract design and contract management encourage participation? Are there steps that can be taken to promote more democratic or substantive participation? This will require some consideration of the different constructs of engagement and variations in democratic processes. Amirkhanyan and Lambright clearly hold to a bottom-up (or direct) view of participation, but other perspectives are worth considering. Second, are there relationships between participation and the performance of governments and contractors? This book shows that contractors may be using participatory mechanisms as a way to validate their performance and secure future contracts. Researchers should investigate this potential conflict of interest, but also look beyond it to ascertain whether participation can be used to influence service delivery outputs and outcomes. This may require developing new variables to measure performance in ways that account for more than cost and post hoc perceptions. Finally, work is needed to identify how contracting out participation affects the legitimacy of the state. At the most basic level, to what extent are citizens able to distinguish between interactions with contractors and interactions with government? Does the use of private firms to gather input affect citizens’ perceptions of government, particularly their satisfaction and trust? Legitimacy is largely derived from the power granted by the people. Participation led by third parties could eliminate a critical interface for the state and reduce its legitimacy. In this excellent book, Amirkhanyan and Lambright wed two important and long understudied areas of public administration scholarship: contract management and public participation. Doubtless, the increasing use of contracts influences the ways that government interacts with citizens. Practitioners and scholars alike need to better understand the democratic ramifications of contracting out. Citizen Participation in the Age of Contracting starts a new conversation about the effects of contracting out. Offering stimulating findings and introducing a topic ripe for future research, the book is likely to become a staple for scholars interested in inter-sectoral management, cross-sector collaboration, and government contracting.

t: Reflections From the Frontier of Behavioral Science and Democratic Governance
abs: Peter John’s latest book, How Far to Nudge?: Assessing Behavioural Public Policy, is part intellectual history, part a tale of policy diffusion, and part a personal reflection on the behavioral science revolution in public policy and administration by someone who himself was one of its key rebels. John, who is a professor of political science and public policy in the United Kingdom, was an early protagonist and practitioner of behavioral and experimental approaches to public administration. In a sense, this book completes a trilogy of volumes by him on the topic: the first, Nudge, Nudge, Think, Think: Experimenting with Ways to Change Civic Behavior (John et al. 2011), documents cases in which John and his collaborators used behavioral insights (such as the tendency to comply with social norms) to test nudge strategies aimed at influencing citizens to recycle, volunteer, vote, and give to charity; in the second, Field Experiments in Political Science and Public Policy (John 2017), John provides guidance on the design and implementation of randomized controlled trials of behavioral interventions involving government programs and services. In How Far to Nudge?, John steps back to reflect more broadly on the origins, practices, limitations, ethics, and political implications of behavioral public policy. As he writes in the introduction: “Given the success of nudge, now is the time to broaden it out and to link it more closely to democratic practice” (p. 14). He begins by making the case that many important social, health, and economic challenges facing government have their roots in both individual and collective human behaviors. Diseases are often determined by health behaviors, for example, although John is quick to point out the structural influences (such as poverty and access to health care) that play a key role in addition to human behavior. Still, he makes a compelling argument for the important role of behavior change in many areas of public policy and administration. Next, he tells the fascinating story of the behavioral revolution in the social sciences. For those already acquainted with popular books such as Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow (Kahneman and Egan 2011), Richard Thaler’s Misbehaving (Thaler and Ganser 2015), and Michael Lewis’ The Undoing Project (Lewis 2016), this story will be somewhat familiar. But John tells it from his own perspective as a political scientist and articulates the connections to public policy and administration. Amusingly, he enjoys cluing his reader in on some of the hype and self-promotion that accounts, at least in part, for the popularity of behavioral economics in the halls of government and in the public imagination. But he pays due respect as well to the important advances and insights of the likes of Kahneman, Amos Tversky, Thaler, Cass Suntein, Daniel Ariely, and others whose work over the years formed the intellectual foundations for behavioral public policy. The middle chapters of the book reflect on the practices and limitations of behavioral policy in government, a narrative informed to a large extent by John’s own extensive work in the United Kingdom and other countries applying nudge strategies to government. He discusses how nudge units were established in government agencies in the United Kingdom (especially the Behavioral Insights Team) and elsewhere and, importantly, how their continuation often depends on the contingencies of political leadership and changing priorities. Usefully, John specifies some of the key (and often unmentioned) limitations of behavioral insights in government, such as the limited range of application (mostly letters, forms, and messages), small and often temporary effects, limited generalizability, and the worry that a focus on nudge diverts the government’s attention from pursuing more substantive (and expensive) solutions to pressing social and policy problems. John also devotes a chapter to the ethics of nudging, which has been defined largely as a form of libertarian paternalism because it entails both choice and direction (nudge). John fully recognizes the dangers inherent in the creation of a “psychological state” but remains optimistic about the potential of nudging, given the generally limited and transparent nature of the nudge initiatives to date and the potential to incorporate nudge tactics into reflective, self-governance practices. Usefully, John also reminds us that public policy-making, in general, involves difficult ethical questions and that nudge is often a less intrusive instrument than laws, regulations, and other conventional instruments of government control over people’s behavior. In the last chapters, as foreshowed throughout the book, John make an original argument: nudges work well enough, but they must be made more open, democratic, and deliberative to truly sustain long-term behavior change and thus improve government and society. “Nudge plus (think)” is what he advocates. This approach envisions a behavioral public policy that leverages both System 1 (fast, intuitive) and System 2 (slow, deliberate) thinking, following Kahneman’s well-known formulation, in the service of better outcomes for individuals and society (Kahneman and Egan 2011). Thus, John highlights ways in which nudge initiatives can incorporate citizen participation and can be made more transparent and explained more fully to citizens. In addition, he makes the point that nudge should not be just a tool of technocrats but should be decentralized to agencies, local governments, and civil society organizations to incorporate behavioral insights into their own autonomous activities. John explains: “The idea is that a combination of nudging and thinking can help the creation of an automated and self-regulating system whereby people get to their goals and where there is a synergy between social and individual aims” (p. 133). But, of course, this formulation is complicated by the implications of the very behavioral revolution John writes about. If we believe what modern psychology has to say about the large role in human behavior played by automatic thought processes (thinking fast), emotions (gut feelings), and our limited capacity for rational problem solving (bounded rationality), then conscious deliberation only gets us so far. The conscious mind is the tip of an iceberg, we have come to discover, consisting of a murky mass of evolutionary or deeply learned associations, construals, heuristics, and biases. But what John argues in his book, it seems to me, is that this conscious tip of the iceberg can nevertheless reflect on how it deals with and attempts to influence the unconscious mass of forces active below the surface. Just like a patient in psychotherapy learns to recognize and deal with the deeply buried emotions that intrude on his life, even if he cannot alter them, so too a democratic society can learn to recognize its cognitive biases and behavioral bugs and find ways, through democratic deliberation, to deal with them and thus live a better collective life. In sum, Peter John’s How Far to Nudge? provides a thoughtful, insightful and original take on the behavioral science revolution in public policy and administration. The book serves as a helpful resource for those looking for an overview of the current status of nudge in government, and it would provide a useful text for graduate courses that include a focus on behavioral public policy and administration. And yet the book is thought-provoking for those already familiar with the topic as well because, having worked extensively at applying nudge tactics in government and having read widely in the behavioral sciences, John is able to provide a uniquely informed perspective on the practices, limitations, ethics, and political implications of the behavioral turn in public policy and public administration as this approach assumes an increasingly prominent role in governments around the world.
